content:
This year on August 9, the Hong Kong Observatory recorded an all-time high of 36.9 degrees Celsius, with Sheung Shui reaching an even higher 39.8 degrees in the early afternoon. In the sweltering heat, I stayed inside the long-shaped apartment, leaving only a narrow gap in the window for ventilation. Under extreme high temperatures, hot air really does surge indoors. So the balcony door and the hall windows were all shut tight. I live on a mid-floor unit between two small hills, and apart from noon, the sun is blocked from all sides. Even without air-conditioning, three ceiling fans creak away, spinning cool air through the apartment. Amid Hong Kong-style heatwaves, one must be grateful.

In the record-breaking heat, I stayed home to do laundry. Shortly after 1 p.m., I washed two large bedsheets with duvet covers, four pairs of jeans and a pile of T-shirts. Two hours later, I turned the bedsheets and covers over to sun-dry the other side. As a result, shortly after 6 p.m., I held the warm laundry like something just pulled out of an industrial washing machine at the dry cleaner's, and laid them on the bed. It felt as if I hadn't experienced such naturally sun-dried, clean clothes in half a century. I should have been worried about my friend under the fierce sun, but only by washing load after load of laundry could I offset, even just a little, the loathsomeness of that scorching sun.

August has become a nightmare. I don't know how many more times it will take to break free from that recurring summer farewell. In a night's dream, I was strutting proudly, twisting my mother along as I walked, saying, 'My little mummy.' I was happily gripping her tight. Then I saw a mysterious woman ahead, draped in a long, deep maroon cloak. Subconsciously I didn't want to see her face clearly, but in the end the dream's camera kept zooming in on her features. She was a strange woman I didn't recognize. Until I woke, the exhilarated feeling welled up, and what I remembered was: I had dreamed of mother again.

On the evening of August 10, 2020, our whole family sang hymns, kissed mother's forehead, and bid her farewell—a complete full stop. Yet letting go is a lesson hard to learn in a lifetime. Reluctance to part is a hidden wound. Six years on, regrets still surface in countless small details, with my mind repeatedly replaying the days six years ago that led to that day.

The regrets and reluctance of parting, sooner or later, regardless of age, will appear at different stages of life. A female student in my writing class wrote in her essay about her late grandmother. It is a piece of remembrance, mourning or regret. When she was even younger, she despised living with her grandmother in the countryside. By day she squabbled with grandmother with the boundless energy of a little imp; grandmother would pinch her ear, and she would strike back, letting grandmother feel the pain she felt too. Then, through a crack in the door, the little girl saw her aged grandmother secretly wiping away tears. That very night, the girl fell ill with fever, and walked dazedly to grandmother, saying, 'I feel awful.'

Feeling awful simply means feeling unwell—it is how a child experiences sickness. She had a high fever, burning all over. Without a word, grandmother found clean clothes for her to change into, and immediately carried her on her back to the hospital to wait to see the doctor. That medicinal oil smell she had once found repulsive, vague and hazy, carried her to the hospital. After a while, somehow the whiff of medicinal oil faded, and the little girl sat alone near the reception desk waiting. Then, some adults asked her, 'Where's your family?' As she spoke, she began to cry, until the scent of medicinal oil drifted close again, and she felt safe and settled as she waited for the doctor to give her an injection and medicine.

Back home, the smell of medicinal oil was there as usual, but seemed to have lost its sharp pungency. From the kitchen came the sound of meat being chopped on a cutting board, and the aroma of rice porridge wafting from the hot wok. The essence of life on earth needs no elaborate explanation—it is this simple and clear.

I wonder, who is cooking porridge for the sick today?

When I was little, it was mostly dad, sometimes mum, who would have the patience to 'mince beef' and cook porridge for me. This was the sick-day menu, and only I got to eat it. Sometimes, after seeing the doctor, I would pre-order this kind of meat porridge: 'I want the beef and scallion porridge.' It was a sick-day privilege. Now, no one cooks this particular dish of porridge for me anymore; when I'm ill, I will no longer get to eat this beef porridge.

'When you're sick these days, just call Food Panda,' a friend said. Other friends will cook plain porridge or fish porridge for their wives. 'Sometimes I cook minced meat porridge too.' 'I chop it by hand, not with a blender.' 'Just a few minutes of chopping.' Because a pot of porridge makes one feel cherished.

'In your whole life, there aren't many people who will cook porridge for you when you're ill. After growing up, the most likely scenario is that you cook it for others. These things, many people have gone through them. No matter what you think, say a proper goodbye, speak from your heart. Those who read it will feel comforted for you too.' I told the girl. She looked at me, and a flicker of light shone in her eyes.

An essay about grandmother can bring comfort. My father, my mother, my grandmother… these are stories we know instinctively how to write.

The girl is not merely a good writer. She seized medicinal oil as her anchor, built around it, and conveyed her true feelings towards her dearest亲人. She need not have loved grandmother the most, but that togetherness arranged by fate makes it impossible for her to forget all that grandmother did for her today, and impossible not to understand that people simply grow up in this unknowing way. In the end, she submitted a piece that was deeply moving and left one feeling 'awful.'

Medicinal oil went from being detestable, to reliable, to shameful, to something to be remembered. It turns out that on the girl's first day of primary school, she was laughed at by classmates for smelling of medicinal oil and called a country bumpkin. She ran home crying and sternly ordered her grandmother to wash every piece of clothing thoroughly with heavy doses of laundry detergent. Grandmother held the clothes and wept. From when the girl was eight months old, grandmother had raised her, until she grew up and went to school, encountering the outside world. The granddaughter became a different person, and hurt grandmother's heart. After returning to live with her mother, one day grandmother had already developed dementia (Alzheimer's disease). The girl went back with her mother to visit grandmother, only to find that she was no longer 'recognized.'

'You can't be my granddaughter; she doesn't like talking to me,' the old grandmother said to the girl.

Life is both real and cruel. Have I ever been this cruel to my mother? It seems not. Or perhaps I have, unknowingly like the girl. Family members sometimes hurt each other. The key is, afterwards, have we come to understand love more deeply?
